newsitem.title: UK: Britain springs surprise with $2.0 billion note.
newsitem.headline: Britain springs surprise with $2.0 billion note.

text.p: Britain raised $2.0 billion on Thursday in a rare appearance in international financial markets, taking dealers by surprise.

The floating-rate deal was only the third time since 1992 Britain has borrowed money other than in sterling or European currency units (Ecu). Britain normally issues fixed-rate government bonds for its financing needs in sterling and Ecu.

"As far as the market is concerned, this is a surprise. That's the way the Bank (of England) prefers to do it," said one trader at a British bank involved in the deal. There has been talk recently that Britain was lining up another large bond but the rumours were vague. Britain launched a $2 billion bond on July 15 to refinance part of a $4 billion loan taken out 10 years ago.

That prior deal sparked speculation Britain would increasingly use international rather than domestic debt markets for funding, particularly with the prospect of a change of government within a year which could weigh on the pound and put upwards pressure on British interest rates.

The Bank of Engand said Thursday's issue would complete the refinancing of the old $4 billion loan and was routine debt management. Although the new deal has a five-year life, Britain has an option to repay investors early, from October 1999.
In late 1992 Britain borrowed in dollars and marks to pay debts run up as the government spent billions of pounds trying to support sterling during a European currency crisis.
